Madam Speaker, the issue of food banks is one that clearly shows the different political philosophies and social policies of Conservatives, New Democrats and Liberals.
Conservatives want to eliminate the need for food banks by ensuring that our social safety net is adequate. We want programs that enhance the dignity and self-esteem of the poor and ensure that they have financial incentives to work and pathways out of poverty.
New Democrats also want to eliminate the need for food banks. They want to eliminate the inequality in incomes in Canada by making everyone poor and chasing business and professionals out of the country. They think people want to work for fun not money.
Liberals want to institutionalize food banks, establish national school lunch programs and provide universal food programs whether people need them or not. That would be financed by a continued massive deficit and escalating national debt at the expense of future generations.

Madam Speaker, earlier this year Canadian government officials and parliamentarians were lobbied by Guatemalan officials on the issue of human rights in Guatemala. The timing was intended to ward off embarrassing international indictments against Guatemala at the annual United Nations Human Rights Commission meetings.
Cynically, the moment the commission meetings in Geneva ended Guatemala's level of human rights violations escalated dramatically. Returning refugee communities composed of indigenous peoples are consistently harassed and intimidated and opposition spokespersons are threatened.
Yesterday the Guatemalan government suspended human rights in the country through imposition of a state of exception. The assembly and judiciary have been suspended and the country's ombudsman is under house arrest. There is concern at the moment for the safety of Guatemalans and Canadians attending human rights and indigenous peoples meetings in Guatemala.
The Canadian government must suspend all bilateral trade and aid initiatives in Guatemala until a full international inquiry into these incidents is held and evaluated. The decades old Guatemalan government tyranny must be confronted and stopped.

May 26, 1993

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the Inuit of the central and eastern Arctic who yesterday signed an historic agreement with the Government of Canada to settle their Nunavut land claim and to establish the new Nunavut Territory.
I am particularly pleased with this achievement because in 1977 I did what I could as minister to encourage and facilitate the advancement of this proposal, and over the years I have given it my full support.
However it is the Nunavut people who deserve full credit because for nearly 20 years they pursued this claim with intelligence, firmness, tenacity, diplomacy and good sense.
This settlement not only establishes the new Nunavut Territory but recognizes the right of the Nunavut people to control their own destiny and at the same time to be full partners in Confederation.
Now it is our job to pass the enabling legislation and to do it as quickly as possible. In this case all parties should get together and approve a plan to assure passage of these bills before the June adjournment. Cheers to the people of Nunavut.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to inform the House that May is Cystic Fibrosis
Month. Cystic Fibrosis, CF, is an inherited disorder that primarily affects the respiratory and digestive systems of children. At present there is no cure for the disease.
Each day includes rigorous therapy and treatment for those suffering from CF. The heartening news is that the median age of survival for CF patients has increased from under 4 to over 30.
Since 1960 the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation has been working to better the lives of those who suffer from this disease. Volunteers and financial supporters work ceaselessly to raise funds for research. The Department of National Health and Welfare is pleased to provide funding to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation through its grants to national voluntary health organizations.
I invite the members of this House and all Canadians to support the work of the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation. I wish the foundation and its volunteers a very successful month.

Madam Speaker, NAFTA has done nothing to stop the slow death that supply management is now facing.
Dairy, egg and poultry farming are all dependent on supply management and are important industries in Canada. Farming is already suffering the effects of cross-border shopping, U.S. dumping of soft fruits and vegetables and now an attack on supply management.
The president of the National Farmers Union, Art Macklin, said it best when he said:
If you don't have the power to restrict lower priced imports from coming into your country, then you can't ensure you're going to be able to keep your best agricultural land in production, or to ensure you can produce a variety of foods-Once this thing (NAFTA) is ratified then control over the food system is turned over to those with financial capital.
If NAFTA turns control of our food system over to those with financial capital then we truly doom the family farm in rural Canada. For Canada to turn its basic food production over to international agribusiness is to turn over part of its sovereignty.

Madam Speaker, it is rare that political parties agree on anything but it happened in Newfoundland last week. They agreed on a resolution urging Ottawa to sink its new fisheries management proposal.
This should speak volumes to the federal fisheries minister who is going to have to answer to future generations for the devastation of the province if he proceeds with legislation tabled on May 20 proposing to give the management boards control over who catches fish and the power to penalize fishermen who break the rules.
Creating independent agencies to manage fish stocks in the manner envisaged is ill advised and is one of the worst moves a fisheries minister could make.

The proposed trade agreement with the U.S. and Mexico is designed to guarantee access by multinational companies to the Canadian economy. Tories do not care whether Canadian workers and their families have guarantees to a safe work place, decent wages or a healthy environment. Only the U.S. government is insisting on

Mr. Speaker, this bill amends the Criminal Code with respect to juvenile prostitution. Specifically, it prohibits Canadians from buying the services of child prostitutes while travelling abroad. Just as drug trafficking and aircraft hijacking done anywhere in the world by a Canadian is a crime for which people can be tried in Canada so would this act become a crime for which people can be tried in Canada.
There are far too many travellers, including Canadians, none I hope from any riding held by a Liberal or a Tory, who are creating a demand for child prostitutes particularly in countries like Thailand, Sri Lanka or the Philippines. The children involved in this trade are often sold by their parents into this occupation and they often have no other means of survival.
Since the governments of some nations refuse to crack down on the practice it seems useful that Canadians not add to the problem. In Canada and other western countries the existence of organizations and lobby groups that campaign to make the sexual practices of paedophiles legal demonstrates that this is not purely an Asian problem. The bill simply tries to make it so that Canadians who indulge in this practice abroad can be prosecuted, albeit with evidentiary problems in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, now that tranquillity has been restored I am not sure whether it is a pleasure or not to embark on this excursion. It is a misnomer that we seem to be calling it a debate on NAFTA when NAFTA, as everyone realizes except the government, is in all probability dead.
I wonder why Canadians are looking a bit bewildered. We have been here for in excess of 24 hours now, almost non-stop, looking rather confused at another government manoeuvre to put something through the House with limited debate. The Ottawa Citizen puts it rather clearly today. It said:
The Conservative government has abused the proceedings of the House so much during its tenure that everyone with detailed knowledge of political behaviour during the period 1984 to 1992 wants reform.
All those aspiring to leadership in the Tory government these days are asking for reform. It would be refreshing if one of those contenders in the race would come forward about this time and say no to this. It would be a breath of fresh air for them to say that this is enough. I think Canadians would have great respect for any of the two or three who see themselves as leading contenders for the job who would do that. It would show sincerity and honesty.
The Ottawa Citizen also says:
Government Orders
If is the most tyrannical government in Canadian history in terms of abusing Parliament.
That is putting it very clearly. The article continues:
The Conservatives have used every possible device to enact their agenda. Despite winning a mere 43 per cent of the national vote in 1988 and undergoing steeply declining popularity since then, they have imposed their dark agenda by the most extensive employment of authoritarian methods in Canadian parliamentary history.
That paints a very clear picture. I do not think anything portrays the arrogance of the current government better than the fact that it is already in the fifth year of a four-year mandate, on its last legs, completely severed from the people that it proposes to represent in this country and on its deathbed it is trying to ram through a three-way deal with Mexico and the United States. We are only pretenders in this game because there is really no game. There is no deal.
This is just a manoeuvre on the part of this government to put something through on another hidden agenda which the Canadian people are expected to believe in and will find out about after.
We have had enough experience in this country in trying to find out what is contained in a deal afterward. It is so typical of the current Prime Minister and his wheeling and dealing.
It reminds me of the high drama that surrounded the Meech Lake accord. I remember so well watching that on a television set in Calgary in 1990. The whole country seemed to depend on whether one person got a phone call through to another person. I often wondered what would happen if the line were busy or the phones were down. That seems to be the level to which things have fallen in this country under Tory leadership.
Canadians must wonder why this atmosphere has gone on for so long, almost five years now. Extending a four-year mandate used to be reserved for critical times such as a war and so on when it was thought to be unwise to have an election. This government in its last days is trying to get another thing that it sees as an accomplishment, one more accomplishment. I think it is more likely to be a kink in its tail just before departure and maybe the nail in the coffin that we have all been waiting for.

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
This is how warped the government's thinking is. Its members might look upon the GST as an accomplishment. All they have to do is go out on the street, go down Wellington Street for a few minutes, and ask how many people think the GST was a great accomplishment.
They might even think of the existing free trade agreement with the United States as an accomplishment. They should walk out and ask any of the unemployed. There are probably some of them standing out in front of the Parliament Buildings right now. Ask them if they think the current free trade agreement with the United States was an accomplishment.
I noticed an article in The Financial Post yesterday that says: "Several big Canadian firms have announced plans to expand in the U.S. Many senior executives expect more Canadian companies to move south".
The article says that Jannock Ltd. is spending $300 million and Interprovincial Pipe Line Systems announced it will spend $1 billion on expansion and acquisition in the United States. Are those accomplishments?
If this NAFTA deal we are supposedly trying to close on is to be looked upon as another accomplishment I do not think Canada can stand too many more of these Tory accomplishments.
The GST was one and the free trade agreement was another. If this is an accomplishment then the Canadian people will have something to say about that. It is just another typically mishandled opportunity railroaded through to distract people from so many other anomalies created by this government over the past five years. What is the rush and what is the real agenda here?
If the government was presenting for approval a three-way deal on which all parties could agree, something that is good for Canada, something that would be good for Canada now and in the future, something that was mutually good for all three parties, then there would be nothing but concurrence and no dispute from this side.
What Canadians do not know, the unknown, is what is wrong with this deal. Particularly when the very hub of the deal, the U.S., has very strong reservations that are
growing and is not likely to sign the deal at all. The mystery is why we are willing to sign something when the discussion has really broken down?
Our Prime Minister has been running around for about a year now with his 24 carat pen all cocked, filled and ready to sign? All he is saying is just steady me a bit, direct me to the chair, show me where to sign and it is okay, trust us. Have we ever been misled by this government before?
Pretty soon there will be the opportunity for which voting Canadians have been waiting for nearly five years now. Putting politics aside just for a minute, I cannot believe that there are not people across there, sincere honest people, who would wonder at the wisdom of signing this NAFTA deal now. This thing is yet to take shape, shapeless as we have found it right from the beginning, and is now being rushed through for some unknown reason. They are saying sign it regardless of what it will finally end up being and trust them. I do not think Canadian people are willing to trust the judgment of this government.
They have had it illustrated so many times. There is a lack of ability to arrange priorities. Look at the $5.8 billion that has been allotted to temporarily fix our DND and equip it with some helicopters, not 500 or 5,000 but 50 helicopters.
In my riding there is a stretch of broken down highway that has taken the lives of about 24 people in the last few years. Two of those helicopters would complete that highway, make it into a four-lane highway leading from highway 401, the main artery across Ontario, into the nation's capital. That is the lack of ability, capacity or the will to prioritize things in this nation that has finally caught up with Canadians.
The Canadian people will not get their priorities wrong on election day. I think we are seeing it happen in the provincial elections in this country.
We saw it again in Nova Scotia yesterday. Perhaps that is a bit unfortunate, but I think the message is coming through. The Conservative government has not provided good government, whether it be federal or provincial and the Canadian people are waiting for their chance to speak.
May 26, 1993

The priority of Canadians on election day will be to get rid of the government, send it packing, send it into oblivion. The very soonest possible opportunity to do that, the better for the sake of Canada and Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad I was able to say yes to that earlier motion. I guess I am happy to rise on this matter. I know the House went all night last night on this bill. It is one
Government Orders
of the more fundamental bills this Parliament certainly is going to have to handle before it terminates either in June or the fall and we have an election.
I rise to obviously echo most of the things that have been said here over the last 24 hours. There is no stronger term that I can use than the obscenity of a government of which I formerly was a member forcing through a bill on a matter of such fundamental importance, the NAFTA free trade agreement with the United States and Mexico.
I was a government member when we had the fight in the 1988 campaign with free trade. Quite frankly it was the most difficult election I ever had. My vote showed it because I went from 12,000 to 2,000. Now the Liberals are licking their chops in my riding thinking they are going to bite me off whenever I run again. Of course, there was a little different tale in the wind then as far as I am concerned. But as everyone knows, at least we had a debate on free trade in 1988. We had a debate in this House.
I have great respect for the government House leader. From a government House leader point of view of ramming things through, he has done a pretty good job. However, I am going to remind him of several quotes from the record of Parliament when he chastised and criticized and condemned the then Liberal government for ramming bills through on time allocation and they only did it one or two times. However, as the member for Leeds-Grenville mentioned, it has never been done more often in recent history than by this government.
My former colleagues are having a leadership contest. I have had exposure to those and they are certainly exciting things. Goodness knows what can happen after a party picks a new leader.
Something really bothers me and frankly, it is one of the reasons I have no hesitation in sitting over here in opposition. Having been a member of that party which really tried to profess in the House and tried to practise this, it was John Diefenbaker who said that Parliament was the place for people to speak and to debate, but it is this party now in government that completely wipes the blotter book with its history and tradition. The public out there are not inert and are not stupid. The Charlottetown Accord proved that. That is the reason the public are more tuned in to some of the leaders of the land.

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
I have been here for a good number of years and I see one of my colleagues who has been here a little longer than I. The rumour perhaps has been confirmed that he might be elevated to a higher place and that is good for him. That means that there are only about three or four of us who are getting close to the barrel in terms of longevity here.
I could try but I have not got the ability to say it like the former right hon. member for Prince Albert did in saying how he loved Parliament. But Parliament is a sham and a charade when we have this type of allocation of time.
When the government House leader moved the allocation order before lunch he convicted himself when he tried to recite all the debate there had been on the NAFTA bill. He spoke of meetings that had been held across the country, subcommittee meetings and different questions that were asked in the House. He even stooped to talk about the statements of members in the House and took the time of the bureaucrats to tally all that. But then he came out with his own words and said what we all know in this House, that the debate on second reading until last night had been four and a half hours.
This bill is fundamental to the future of Canada and North America. That is why I have no hesitation in saying the government is forcing this bill through now. The majority rules, there is no doubt about that. I would love to see certain reforms of Parliament that everyone is preaching about. In effect there may be some way to control the allocation and get a discretion in the Speaker.
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, as you well know I had grave misgivings when this matter was moved into committee under closure and you decided you had to put the motion. I certainly was hoping the government would delay putting the motion so there could have been some more debate before it was forced into a committee. It sat only on technical evidence. It did not call outside evidence. It did not visit different parts of the country. It really just cleaned up some of the definitions of this 4,400 page bill rather than really analysing some of the pluses and minuses that go behind the bill.
We are debating this in this House today when there is going to be a leadership convention. We all know this House is going to most likely be cut off by the guillotine and perhaps not come back after the leadership convention. The first big question the new leader is going to
have to pick for the present government is whether it is going to expose itself to the House of Commons in its habit of forcing everything through by abusing the allocation rule.
I have been here under many reforms of Parliament. The allocation rule is only to be used to allocate time after there has been a good old filibuster, after there has been obstruction or after there has been a very definite effort on the part of the members of Parliament and/or the opposition in concert to really thwart the passage of a bill. You cannot say that, Mr. Speaker, when there has only been four and a half hours before closure came in to ram it into committee. Then it comes out of committee and we have it here in an all-night session last night.
I do not know who is doing what to whom, but I know what is happening. The Prime Minister is bowing off the stage. We are not sure what the Minister for International Trade is doing at the moment, but there is some rumour that he may be bowing off the stage too.
Former friends and colleagues of mine on the government side who would not debate this in their caucus should ask the Prime Minister, the Minister for International Trade and the government House leader if they remember when they were in opposition and used to champ at the bit in those rare times when the then Liberal government forced things through and they said things about the rape of Parliament and how people were being ignored. Have they forgotten from whence they came?
I want to read just one little excerpt from the speech of the member for Calgary Centre as he then was before he became government House leader in a debate in this House. I have so many more, Mr. Speaker. This is Bill C-78 an act to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, which caused quite a lot of controversy around here. After days of debate the government moved allocation and this is what the member for Calgary Centre, the present government House leader said about closure:
"Mr. Speaker, this motion by the government to close off debate is despicable and outrageous. It is all of those adjectives that could and should be used to describe it. But perhaps more than that, it is tragic in a real sense that more than just this bill is involved, more than just the vitally important national energy policies are involved. It is really one more nail if you will, one more bit of pressure on what little parliamentary democracy we have".
May 26, 1993

I have another quote from page 6157, but my time is just about up. Mr. Speaker, I will not presume any further. I appreciate you recognizing me because I frankly could be voting for many parts of the NAFTA bill. I must say I am upset with the drug part that is incorporated in this international agreement. I have no hesitation, in view of the process the government has used, of voting against this bill in every form and campaigning against it because it has not been fair to Canadians to do it this way.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is appropriate that a member from Prince Albert stand up after the remarks from the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants because Prince Albert has always been identified very strongly with the sanctity of Parliament and with parliamentarians and politicians representing ordinary Canadians. It has been identified very strongly with integrity in political life, all of which is missing in the government's performance with respect to the NAFTA legislation.
Certainly what we are engaged in today could be called the theatre of the absurd. This is not Parliament any more. This is a total absurdity for a number of reasons.
The first is the overriding of parliamentary debate, national debate and the rights of people to have their parliamentarians debate their issues in Parliament by the action of closure that this government has indulged in again.
This is the fortieth or forty-fifth time that we have had time allocation or closure since we came to this House in 1988. The government has used closure more times in this Parliament than in the whole history of Canada to this point. Surely we need no further evidence of the contempt with which this government holds the Canadian people and the contempt it has for this institution.
To think that many of these members originally traced their political roots to the former member from Prince Albert, John Diefenbaker, really does reinforce the point that these people have strayed a long, long way from their roots and have very little sense of their own history. They have very little sense of the political
Government Orders
movement that brought them to power and kept the Conservative Party alive through the dark years until they could finally become a government. It is a legacy which they have now betrayed.

speechtext: He would be rolling over in his grave.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
He would indeed. The member says that former Prime Minister John Diefenbaker would be rolling over in his grave and that is indeed the truth.
This is the theatre of the absurd because we are passing a piece of legislation that does not even exist in many ways. It does not exist because this is an agreement among three countries: Canada, the United States and Mexico. Only in Canada, like the commercial says, are we ploughing ahead with this legislation before we even know what it is.
Certainly Mexico has taken the position that the legislation should go forward as it is. But the major trading partner in this agreement that no country can proceed without is the United States of America. As we all know the Americans are bogged down in their own debate on this issue. There is no guarantee whatsoever that this legislation will even be passed by the Americans. Certainly if it is passed by the Americans it will not be in anything like the form we see it in today.
What possible reason could there be for rushing this legislation through under closure to implement a piece of legislation that in the end will not even be the actual agreement which comes to the table to be agreed upon by the three countries? This really is a farce and a travesty of democracy that we are engaged in today.
The specific motion that is on the table right now is Motion No. 4 and I would like to turn to that for just a minute. It is a motion that stands in the name of the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, the trade critic for our party. I would like to pay tribute to that member because through the long months and years preceding this debate there have been many times when that member was virtually the only person of any stature going around the country alerting Canadians to the dangers which we again face through this agreement.

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
I am very pleased that this motion stands in his name because as we propose to amend this particular motion, it states that nothing in this act or the agreement shall be interpreted so as to prohibit a party to the agreement from requiring the processing of raw materials or raw resources before exporting such materials or resources.
I think this particular motion really gets to the heart of one of the key issues in the whole free trade regime be it the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement or this agreement among Canada, Mexico and the United States. It is the ability of our country to process our resources that is going to make our economy work in the future.
In an era of globalization with value added processing of knowledge industries, of secondary processing, it is the ability to use our resources to enjoy maximum benefits that will make it possible for us to have a functioning economy in this country in the future.
I think it is instructive to look back at the last election. I think the people in the hinterlands, the resource producing regions, understood very well at that time what the whole free trade philosophy and debate was all about.
After the last election I contemplated what I might say in that debate in December 1988.1 was trying to think of what could be said that had not already been said. I looked at the recent electoral map at that time in which the NDP constituencies were outlined in orange, the Liberal constituencies were in red and the Conservative constituencies were in blue. Looking at that map it struck me that virtually the whole map looked red and orange. There was very little blue there in spite of the fact that the Conservatives had won the government.
I put a researcher to work for half a day and added up the square kilometres per constituency for each of the parties and came out with a very interesting finding. We found that only 15 per cent of the land mass of Canada is represented by the government, while 85 per cent of the land mass of this great country is represented by the opposition.
That vast land mass contains the resource producers: the farmers, the fisher-persons, the people engaged in
forestry and the miners. These are the people who know how the economy of this country works or does not work. These are the people who dig up the raw resources and enjoy the few benefits that come from doing that. They see those resources shipped out of the country through the ports to foreign countries to be processed.
People in the resource-producing regions in agriculture, fishing, mining or forestry know that is the fundamental weakness of this country. They also know that with the control the Americans have gained over our resources through the free trade agreement it is impossible to create those kinds of structures, institutions and regulatory requirements that will allow us to use our own resources for our own benefit in the future development of this country.
Then the government promised it would bring in the finest adjustment mechanisms to compensate for the fall-out from free trade that has been seen in many places in the world. What a farce it was to talk about adjustment mechanisms. It was a farce right across the country, but it was particularly a farce in the resource producing regions and the hinterlands in this country. Many of these resource producing regions depend on seasonal employment. They depend on self-employment in the case of farmers and fisher-persons and others. In many cases there are also aboriginal communities that have structural unemployment that has gone back a long way.
What did the government do? It took the training money that used to be available to everybody in this country from the UI fund to train UI recipients. The net effect is that the training money in this country now goes to those fewer urban areas where there are enough people on UI to warrant those kinds of expenditures while the outlying regions, the hinterlands, have been nixed in the training funding in this country.
My own constituency absorbed a cut this year of about $1.5 million in training money available. It is one of the poorest constituencies in the country with 25 per cent to 40 per cent unemployment depending on how one considers it.
There are a few other things I was going to put on the record. I question again what the Liberals think: they can negotiate in renegotiating the free trade deal.

The Americans say they are after our wheat, pork, steel and lumber. If that is what we want to renegotiate with then what kind of negotiating position is that? It is a total non-starter and people should know it.
However the last thing I would like to say is that what has bedevilled us in this debate has been the division of forces and the political opposition over this agreement. I think Canadians should see that in spite of the noise the Liberals make that they are wobbling on this question. They also see that we have a national party in the field that is dividing it one more time.
If we want to stop these agreements then the only thing to do is unite behind the New Democratic Party in the next federal election.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to participate in the limited debate the government is allowing on Bill C-115, an act to implement the North American free trade agreement.
Given the significance of NAFTA, members on this side of the House and Canadians in general are not impressed by the actions of the government in ramming through this important piece of legislation.
The three days of debate allotted from report stage, third reading and passage does not give members sufficient time to put forward their constituents' views on NAFTA.
The proposals in NAFTA will alter the way of life of all Canadians. Using the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement as a guide, NAFTA's implementation will have a negative impact on Canada.
In my riding of Stormont-Dundas I have seen what the Conservative government's version of free trade means for Canada. It means high unemployment, plant closures and an exodus southward of Canadian businesses owned by foreign parent companies and a Canadian economy near ruin.
Under the FTA Canada was placed on the verge of losing its economic sovereignty. There is little talk from the present government of guaranteed access to the U.S. marketplace and the jobs, jobs, jobs that were to flow from the FTA.
Everyone knows that Canada has come out the big loser under the FTA. The U.S. used every trade-inhibiting tactic it could think of to prevent shipments to the
Government Orders
south of Canadian-made products: softwood lumber, steel, pork and the list goes on.
It did not matter to the U.S. if there was a genuine grievance or not. By slapping on increased duties and tariffs the damage inflicted on our markets in the U.S. would be done as our products became prohibitively expensive to purchase.
At the same time any U.S. companies wishing to take advantage of Canadian markets were given red carpet access.

The Liberal Party insisted that the main focus of our government during the trilateral negotiations should be to protect Canada's interests and to correct the flaws contained in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. By pretending that NAFTA represents a marked improvement, not only do the Conservatives admit to their own failure, but they prompt us to be sceptical.
The government's main objective when it negotiated the free trade deal was to secure free access to the American market. It failed miserably. Because of a lack of codes in NAFTA, our companies are once again exposed to trade sanctions on the part of the United States. Just remember what happened with softwood lumber, steel and magnesium.

In 1988 the Prime Minister promised massive adjustment programs to help Canadian companies and workers adjust to the FTA. We all know that these adjustment programs never materialized. Now under the FTA there are no programs to create jobs and to facilitate Canadian workers in adapting this new unimproved trade deal.
There are efforts being taken today at reaching side deals to NAFTA on environmental and labour standards. The Government of Canada should consider undertaking a side deal to NAFTA itself.
Hopefully something will come out of these side deals to address these two important concerns. However, given the government's previous failures one should not be too optimistic.
While the FTA's trade dispute panels have been made permanent under NAFTA, the decisions made by these panels are not binding in all cases. Moreover, nothing in NAFTA accelerates the lengthy and expensive dispute settlement process. The flaws contained in both the FTA and NAFTA will still continue to deter both fair and free trade between Canada, the United States and Mexico.

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
I referred earlier to the economic problems in my riding of Stormont-Dundas. I have witnessed the negative impact the FTA has had on communities throughout eastern Ontario and especially in Cornwall. Unemployment in the city stands at over 20 per cent with plant closures causing the loss of over 3,000 quality jobs in the last two years.
In addition, the Nestle plant located in Chesterville and Dundas county was a scene of a six-week lockout by the company when its workers refused to accept a new contract which included a so-called continental work week. This permits a company to eliminate premium pay for work done on weekends.
The company said it needed this flexible work week if it was to maintain its competitiveness in the U.S. market. Continental work weeks appear to be the norm in plants located in the U.S., including Nestle's sister plants down south. As the company exports 70 per cent of its products to the U.S., it told its employees that it would require a continental work week to hold on to its markets in the face of increasing competition, including its own plants in the U.S.
The Nestle dispute is the future face of business in Canada under NAFTA. Canadian workers will be forced to accept things like the continental work week in order for Canadian products to keep their U.S. markets. In addition, Canadian workers will continue to lose their jobs with NAFTA as they have under the FTA as companies continue streamlining operations in order to remain competitive.
It is impossible for Canadian businesses exporting to the U.S. and Mexico to produce products cheaper than those made in the U.S. and Mexico. The cost of manufacturing similar products in the U.S. and Mexico is lower and foreign multinationals know this. Today we maintain markets by the quality of our products and our business ingenuity, but there is no escaping the difficulties that are ahead under NAFTA.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party is convinced that Canadians can be successful in the global economy, providing the government supports them with sound economic policies instead of throwing them to the wolfes
like the Conservatives did. We recognize that international trade is critical to job creation in Canada.

Canadian businesses, Canadian products and Canadian workers can compete with the best in the world. However this government has not kept its part of the bargain to provide fair trade and stimulate economic growth. The economic policies of the present government have consistently failed. The government has created hardship for our industries and it has led to unemployment instead of increased economic progress. The previous high dollar, high interest rate policies of this government, coupled with excessive taxation, the GST, the FTA and now NAFTA demonstrate the damage this government has inflicted on Canada's economy.
I urge the members of the cabinet of this government to take a drive down main street Canada. Come and visit Cornwall and other cities throughout Canada. The government should see the results of its economic mismanagement. Perhaps it will realize that, like NAFTA, it has failed to protect Canadian industry. It has failed to protect Canadian jobs and has failed to offer any solutions to bring about a better and brighter economic future for the country.
In conclusion, NAFTA cannot bring about a reversal of nine years of Conservative economic failure. Only a new government can address myriad problems created by members opposite. I call upon this House to reject NAFTA and for the government to go to the Canadian people in an election so that the people can get a government committed to getting Canada working again.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for this opportunity to speak on the government bill to implement the North American free trade agreement.
I believe that the government's attitude toward democracy is abominable, even atrocious and that it is most insulting to the Parliament of Canada. Why is it hustling us, why is it pressuring us into voting after only a few hours of debate on this particular bill? Why is the government rushing Canada into an agreement with the United States and Mexico when everyone knows that the Americans are not ready to ratify it this year? Everyone knows full well that Congress will not deal with this issue until late fall.
May 26, 1993

Why is the government pressuring us? We all know that the government's mandate is in its fifth year, that the Prime Minister handed in his resignation and that the Conservative Party is now looking for a new leader. In about three weeks, Parliament will probably be adjourned until fall.
Why is the government in such a rush to impose closure on the debate, preventing parliamentarians from voicing their views on the North American free trade agreement? We know that the Americans are quite concerned about some issues as they relate to the agreement. The new American president served notice to Mexico and Canada that there will be a new side agreement on top of the one agreed to by the former prime minister. We know very well that this agreement contains serious flaws, extremely damaging to the North American continent.
We need job security and we need to protect the working conditions of our labour force. It is very important that this be included in the agreement, which is not the case now. There is nothing in it on the environment. What about the government's green plan? Does it not respect its own plan? Why is it not dealing with this issue in the bill on NAFTA?

The Liberal Party is for free trade. It is for freer trade and it is also for fair trade. We need an agreement which has rules. The Liberal Party's stand on NAFTA has the following six principles to guide it.
First, we must correct the flaws in the FTA. The government should use the opportunity, with the U.S. and Mexico, to correct the flaws in the original Canada-U.S. trade deal. For instance, the dispute settlement mechanism has proved to be time consuming and costly and it is not binding in all trade disputes. The mechanism is due to phased out in seven years.
The NAFTA should also address sectors which are important to Canada such as financial services and government procurement sectors. They were not adequately treated in the FTA. Canada's principal objective in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was to secure access to the American market, and more important,
Government Orders
exemptions from the U.S. countervail and anti-dumping laws. As the Honda, softwood and steel cases have shown, that objective was not achieved in the FTA. The error must not be repeated in the NAFTA. At the same time, Canada's social, cultural and regional development programs must be secured in any agreement.
Before an agreement takes place, the government should establish comprehensive adjustment programs for business and labour. In 1988 the government promised massive adjustment and assistance programs to help firms and workers adjust to the reality of free trade. Yet in the last four years, there have been no initiatives in this crucial area.
The trilateral agreement must entrench meaningful environmental, labour and health standards. Canadian standards cannot be allowed to fall to the lowest common denominator in a North American trading arrangement. Nor should health, safety and environmental standards be employed as hidden barriers to trade.
Any NAFTA should include internationally recognized standards, enforceable through the dispute settlement mechanism. In crucial areas such as the environment, we should make the NAFTA a model of other multilateral trade arrangements such as the GATT.
The government should ensure that the agreement is symmetrical so that Canada is not asked to cede more than Mexico. For example it seems unlikely that Mexico will agree to open its energy sector to the extent that Canada did under the original FTA.
Finally the agreement should make it possible for Canada's other western hemisphere trading partners to join the trade area without delay and time consuming negotiations.

That is why I will vote against this bill that the government is ramming down our throats just as it did with the GST and the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States a few years ago. Why is this government always insisting on operating as if it were a board of directors? Does it not have any respect for the Parliament of Canada where freedom of speech should prevail? Is the government afraid to engage in a national debate with all the stakeholders?

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
It is quite obvious that the government is in a big hurry and that it wants to pressure us for the third time, after the free trade agreement and the GST, into an agreement, NAFTA, that even the United States are not ready to pass.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say how pleased I am to see you in the chair, but regret the circumstances that necessitate you being there in the absence of our Speaker Fraser. I hope that all is going well with him.
Because I have limited time and will not be able to focus on all of my amendments, I want to do as I have done in the past and pick out one particular amendment to argue why this bill should not pass the House and how ill-conceived the bill is in terms of caring for the Canadian people.
My amendments deal with the fact that NAFTA is being used by corporate lobbyists and the U.S. government to rectify the lack of a formal intellectual property code in the free trade agreement. It is no coincidence that the first major industrial association to endorse NAFTA was the U.S. Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association.
Why do I say that? It is not because it is a matter of political rhetoric, but it is a matter of fact that the earlier legislation that was passed in this House in favour of a monopoly control of pharmaceutical drugs and intellectual property, protecting themselves and giving them

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
massive access to profits goes hand and hand with this bill.
When I make the charge that NAFTA is being used by corporate lobbyists and the U.S. government to rectify the lack of formal intellectual property code in the FTAI need to have a reference. The reference I use is from page 41 of "Which Way for the Americas Analysis of NAFTA Proposals that Impact on Canada" published by the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives in co-operation with Common Frontiers and Action Canada Network. I quote page 41: "The PMA believes that NAFTA patent provisions go beyond the draft GATT. Text on trade-related intellectual property rights lock in changes to Mexico's patent laws and cementing the proposed changes to Canada's patent legislation contained in Bill C-91".
For the second time control of the Canadian drug costs are being sacrificed by the Tories in haste to sign a trade deal with the United States.
In 1986 Bill C-22 extended patent protection for brand name prescription drugs that was passed in this House at the insistence of the United States with the support of the multinational pharmaceutical association as well as the Tory backbenchers who were obviously influenced by the multinational pharmaceutical industry.
This particular small, largely unemotional amendment back in 1986 led to the set-up of the pharmaceutical monopoly bill that was passed by this government, C-92, earlier this year and now frozen in stone forever in NAFTA guaranteeing massive profits to the pharmaceutical industry in this country, fought so vigorously by my colleague from the constituency of Surrey North. Day after day he exposed in this House exactly what kind of creeping monopoly control was taking place over the pharmaceutical industry in this country aided and abetted by the Conservative Party for Lord knows what political reason, but obviously some influence by the pharmaceutical association, particularly in the United States.
A war chest? A drug chest? Who knows, but certainly the influence was there.
I am not suggesting the government was under the influence of the lobbyists' products, but they certainly were under the influence of the lobbyists. Perhaps a defence would be that they were under the influence of
the products, but I leave that for the Canadian voters to decide.
This government has set out to enrich those companies to the point that it is estimated a minimum cost annually may reach some $400 million across Canada in extra costs for pharmaceutical prescription drug charges in this country. At a time when this government is preaching restraint, when it is cutting back on services left and right across this country, it is handing a monopoly control situation over to the international drug cartels fronted essentially by American interests.
There has never been a justification why intellectual property and pharmaceuticals should be enshrined in protection to the drug companies under NAFTA. It has just been slipped in there.
Some suggest that there may be a link to former President Ronald Reagan's closest private sector trade adviser who is Edmund Pratt, chairperson of Pfizer and Company, a leading U.S. multinational pharmaceutical drug company. Pratt was the chairperson of the U.S. Trade Representatives Advisory Committee and the chairperson on the Emergency Committee for American Exports.
The connection is there and it is obvious. There is nothing new that I am revealing here about that connection.
Furthermore, on February 26, 1992 a letter to the U.S. Trade Representative Carla Hills and the members of the intellectual property committee that I spoke of said and I quote: "In clear straightforward language the NAFTA must require Canada to dismantle its discriminatory licensing regime for pharmaceutical products and suspend the guaranteeing of any compulsory licences from December 20, 1990 onward". Both of these demands were met when the Conservatives tabled Bill C-91. As a consequence of that lobbying and that pressure and the direct connection between United States interests and the pharmaceutical companies this government rushed to act. It was unseemly haste.
Would it react to the unemployed in this country with that haste? Would it react to the many small businesses that have gone broke in this country with the same haste? Would it help the elderly, the poor, or the children of this country who need help with succour and comfort from the government to be totally ignored but
May 26, 1993

when the American drug companies came calling they got what they wanted?
It was a remarkable set of actions put into place by massive lobbying from the U.S. interests particularly through the letter to the U.S. trade representative, Carla Hills.
It is a shame. I repeat that I am only picking out one small part of this particular amendment that would correct these kinds of obscene favouritisms that have been shown in protecting intellectual property.
Furthermore, on page 16 of the government's own analysis of the North American free trade agreement under the section on intellectual property there is a section protecting the pharmaceutical companies and the agribusiness companies from disclosure of the efficacy of any one of the drugs or pharmaceutical products or agribusiness chemicals that they produce.
In other words they can now keep secret from public health departments any research they do on a pharmaceutical drug or a pesticide or any agribusiness chemical product, any research they have done to show that the efficacy may be harmful to people or to animals or environmentally damaging. Those documents done by those companies would no longer be subpoenable, no longer available to the public.
Let me give an example of what I am saying. The tragedy in Bophal, India, by the massive U.S. chemical interests and the death of over 4,000 people by the dispensation, somewhat illegally, of poison toxic fumes into the atmosphere killing those people in India, has led to massive litigation in India and in the United States. It was painfully slow, terribly unsuccessful, but at least there was a process for the people in Bophal, India, to go back after that chemical company.
Should this pass I warn every single Canadian citizen that we will give up the right to subpoena in court or to be made available to any public health officer the information that the company may have on the efficacy of a drug or an agribusiness chemical product.
We are saying this is not a Third World country we are dealing with here in Canada and these are not the kind of abuses we have seen catalogued to Third World countries by multinational chemical companies. A sophisticated country like Canada or the United States will
Government Orders
now be subject to the secrecy of the drug companies and any of the research they do.
I do not exaggerate. This is a fact. It is there on page 16 of the government's own summary. We are abandoning to the Canadian people access to information as to drug safety and efficacy.
Who asked for this? Who is it that asked that this protection for the companies and the lack of protection for the citizens be put in the bill? Governments never answered that question. Come to your own conclusion.
I tell you this, Mr. Speaker, God forbid should there be a major chemical incident in this country like Bophal, should there be a repeat of Minamata on an industrial disease scale such as there was in Japan, should there be a relentless effort by some irresponsible corporation to pour toxic fumes into the air, on the soil and in the water, when the time comes for reckoning they will be protected.
In conclusion let me say I do not think this government has the right to take that protection away without at least an explanation of who it is it really cares about. Children, women, men, adults, seniors or the drug companies. Whose side is this government on?

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this amendment I am doing so as a further means of stating my opposition to the NAFTA legislation. I think it relevant to look again at what has happened under the U.S.-Canada free trade deal which is being rolled over into the North American free trade arrangement.
Conservatives have been boasting about the increase in our exports to the United States in recent years. They say that this has happened because of the U.S.-Canada free trade arrangement. However 80 per cent of our exports to that country went there duty free before the U.S.-Canada free trade deal started. They were steadily growing before that time. It seems to me that most of the recent increase in exports would have happened in any event.
Also there are other factors that have been encouraging our exports to the United States. There has been the recent and long overdue decline in the value of the Canadian dollar, making our exports more competitive in the United States. There have been the lower interest

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
rates, also long overdue, which have helped reduce costs and which have also made our export prices better.
I believe claims about increased exports resulting from the North American free trade arrangement coming into effect, if it ever does, have to be taken with a very big grain of salt.
Did all the job losses and closed plants in recent years come about because of the Canada-U.S. free trade deal? Well, we have also had the recession deliberately induced by Conservative policies and what is called a restructuring of the world economy.
However I do believe that the free trade deal with the United States certainly was an important and tragic factor in the losses of hundreds of thousands of jobs and the great number of closed plants since that free trade deal came into effect. That deal did not prevent these tragic developments and in my view made the situation worse.
An example of the pressures on Canadian business created by this trade deal is, as I said earlier today, what is happening with respect to the huge Canadian steel company, Dofasco. It recently announced that it is opening a new steel mill, not in Hamilton or elsewhere in Canada, but in Kentucky. Explaining why the company decided to do this, according to The Financial Post, the company's president said locating in the United States also avoided "the problems of all these stupid trade disputes". The free trade deal with the United States did not end those disputes, it exacerbated them.
A more recent report in The Financial Post with the headline "Canadian companies head to U.S." said:
One big reason for the southern shift, executives say, is free trade.
According to a recent survey of 1,000 senior executives by KPMG
Peat Marwick Thorne, 73 per cent believe North American free
trade will cause plant closures or relocations over the short term.
In other words, the unfortunate trends that we have seen under the U.S-Canada free trade deal are going to continue. They are going to be accentuated if NAFTA comes into effect.
The godfather of the original Canada-U.S. free trade deal and the godfather of NAFTA, the present minister of industry and trade, is backing the Minister of National Defence in the Tory leadership race. That is because he believes that she, above all, will carry out most fully his
policies, the policies of the present Conservative government, measures like the GST, the U.S.-Canada free trade deal and NAFTA. The other leading contender, the Minister of the Environment, also supports these failed policies.
Even if the Conservatives use their majority as they are intending to do to force through a vote on this NAFTA legislation tomorrow, it will still be part of the black record of the Conservative government for which the new Conservative leader and all Conservative candidates in the next election will have to bear responsibility.
I have to ask again, if that is the case, why have the final vote in the House before we know if there is to be any parallel accords dealing with issues like labour standards and the environment? Will they cover all areas of concern to Canada? Will they do so in terms sufficiently serving Canada's interests? We will not know anything about this at the time the Conservatives force this legislation to a final vote by misusing their majority at 5 p.m. tomorrow.
Why have this vote, as I have said before, if we do not know yet whether President Clinton of the United States will ever present the NAFTA legislation to his Congress and, if he does, whether the Congress will pass it? Surely it is not in Canada's interest to have the Conservative majority force this legislation through the House tomorrow before knowing the answers to these questions.
Every poll confirms that Canadians do not want this NAFTA deal as negotiated by this Conservative government. However Canadians recognize that our country is and must be a trading nation. They do not want walls built around it, trying to shut it off from the world as the NDP appears to do. Canadians want, at least as a first step, efforts to renegotiate the trade deals. They believe if there are fair rules and a fair deal when it comes to trade with the United States and the world-the FTA and NAFTA are not fair deals; they are not composed of fair rules-Canadians can compete with the United States, with Mexico and with the world. For this to happen they need a federal government which will stand up for them and stand up with them in order to get fair trading rules and a fair deal when it comes to trade with the United States, Mexico and other countries of the world.
May 26, 1993

I believe Liberals have the commitment and the program to stand up for Canada and stand up for Canadians.
The government says that passing this bill tomorrow will not harm Canada's ability to negotiate side agreements on issues like the environment, labour standards and other relevant matters with the Americans and the Mexicans. It flies in the face of common sense to say that having this bill pass now will not remove some of the bargaining strength of our country. If this bill were not passed Canada could say: "If you do not make a deal that is in our interest we will not present it to our House of Commons".
Once the bill is passed this bargaining tool is gone. The government may say: "We can always refuse to proclaim it", but the government will have already tipped its hand as to the kind of arrangement it will live with. In any event, once the bill is passed changes cannot be made to react to changes in the American legislation or the Mexican legislation without bringing the bill back and reopening the matter.
Again I say it makes no sense to try to force the bill through tomorrow. Also I suggest any parallel accord will likely require new legislation in the House anyway.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:

May 26, 1993

The question is to what degree do Mexico and Canada export similar products to the United States because the United States is our biggest client. Some 85 per cent of our industries export their products to the United States. Mexico is also a major trading partner of the United States.
In 1985 almost 30 per cent of Canadian exports to the United States had competition from Mexico. By 1990 almost 44 per cent of Canadian exports to the U.S.A. were similar to those from Mexico. Therefore, with or without a NAFTA Canada and Mexico are becoming greater competitors with each other to get into the United States market.
If we were to only permit a Mexico-U.S.A. agreement and not involve Canada would this not give Mexican companies more special advantages than exist today? The Canada West Foundation said this about the NAFTA:

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
Canadian direct flows with Mexico are extremely modest, but the question of concern to Canadian trade officials should be the possible displacement of Canadian exports by Mexican exports resulting from a U.S.A.-Mexico only bilateral trade agreement.
People will probably want a concrete example, and this one is in the area of auto parts. Canada exports auto parts to Mexico. However Mexico ships not only auto parts but also motor vehicles to Canada. Canada does not export any vehicles to Mexico because nobody else does. Currently under Mexican law there is an embargo on the importation of motor vehicles. Shortly we will be able to ship cars into Mexico because of recent changes made to the Mexican automotive decree and under NAFTA that will continue and the market will open up further.

If the NAFTA is not in existence, but the U.S. and Mexico arrange their own bilateral deal, then in all likelihood that 10 per cent tariff for American part producers would be eliminated and what will we have left then? We will have the Canadian part producers still having to pay the 10 per cent tariff to get their parts into Mexico, but the American company will not have to pay that 10 per cent tariff which would make American parts cheaper. Therefore Canada would over a period of time lose the $100 million worth of auto parts business that exists today.
That is a concrete example of why Canada decided to join the Mexicans and the United States. If it was just a bilateral agreement with the United States as the hub, that would be a tremendous disadvantage to Canadians and everybody recognizes that.
Everyone talks about why do we want to trade with Mexico, why can we not trade with the European Community. When the subcommittee on external affairs looked at the NAFTA and travelled across the country, when we were in Moncton, Connors Brothers, the people that produce Brunswick sardines made an interesting presentation. That company catches the sardines and packages them in its facility in New Brunswick. All
the value added goes into the sardine can. The company has now gone to Mexico because with some 85 million people, while not all of them are affluent, it has determined that its market size is 25 million people who are able to buy the sardine product. That is the population of Canada, 25 million people.
Brunswick is now shipping sardines and selling successfully into Mexico. The point is that it is doing it out of its facility in New Brunswick where all the value added is. It is getting into that market early. Right now it is paying a 20 per cent tariff which it knows will be eliminated after NAFTA comes into place, but it wants to get into that market now before the Americans get down there.
What happens when this same company wants to sell its canned sardines into the European Community? It has to send the raw fish to Aberdeen, Scotland where then the value added, the canning, takes place and then it can sell from Aberdeen into the European Community.

The FTA's non-wool fabric textile import quota expired at the end of 1992 but was temporarily extended to the end of 1993. The NAFTA will enlarge this quota and make it permanent. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have at least this opportunity to speak. I will do so in general and perhaps somewhat different terms in some respects than others who have spoken with respect to the North American free trade agreement and its twin the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States.
However, I could not approach this topic without observing, as others have observed, that never in the history of Canada has a government acted with such contempt for this place, such contempt for the Constitution of this country and with such contempt for the people that this government is supposed to represent. Never before in the history of this place has there been levied upon it such abuse in the form of time allocation or closure as this government has accomplished in four years of a near dictatorship which is a deep offence to Parliament, to me, to my colleagues in this party, I think to all members of this House and certainly it will be learned on election day to all of the people in this country.
It is very interesting to listen to this debate. As the Conservative member who just spoke, many on that side, as well as in the Liberal Party, continue to talk about the North American free trade agreement and its twin, the free trade agreement, as if all we are talking about are
tariffs and larger markets, prosperity to be gained through competition.
What we are talking about is something far more fundamental than this. Many have talked about the death of social democracy, the notion that says that governments should act on behalf of all of its citizens to ensure that equity and economic prosperity go together, what the free trade agreement is a part of and what NAFTA is a part of. It is a whole series of arrangements that began with the Liberal government and only culminated with the the Conservative government to free transnational corporations from any limits that might be imposed by governments, to free them from any obligations that they may have to nations or to people.
What we are creating is a situation in which transnational corporations will be free to sell, invest, build factories or move jobs wherever they choose in the interests of competition.
This is a process that began with the Liberal Party, that began with the reconstruction of the tax system so that it would benefit the large corporations and the wealthy at the expense of all the rest back in 1975, thus bringing the deficit and all of the harm that that has caused. The specifics of free trade were promoted by a Liberal who chaired the Macdonald commission.
The Liberals talk about these deals as if there were merely trade deals. I cannot believe they are missing the point. We are talking about a fundamental change in the Constitution of the country and a fundamental change among governments, corporations and people in general.
We have in these deals an accord of complete freedom to the transnational corporations to seek the lowest wages, and they have; to seek the lowest levels of taxation and support of programs to benefit the people, and they have; to seek the lowest environmental standards; and to seek the lowest health standards.
The people in my city know the results of following the possibility of moving where labour is cheap and profits are great. My city has experienced the loss of a great many factories and a great many jobs. We could talk about Kelsey-Hayes, Windsor Bumper, the GM transmission plant, and on and on.

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
It is true in recent months Windsor has been a beneficiary of some significant investment for which we thank the Ontario government, a government severely strapped by the situation that has been created. Provincial governments have had their degree of freedom to serve the people severely limited precisely because the corporate agenda has been successful in disarming governments in their effort to protect and serve the people.
We hear the Liberals citing, as we have cited, the heavy toll of unemployment: 1.6 million Canadians and 2.5 million more dependent upon social assistance. Deficits plague all governments because revenues have fallen and costs have risen. Who pays for this? It is not the corporations. The Ontario government will dare not raise the taxes on companies because the companies could flee to Mexico or the United States by virtue of the free trade agreement and NAFTA as well.
They sit watching this misery in full cognizance of the purpose of the corporate agenda which the Conservatives have completed. It is nothing but an arrangement to ensure the easy movement of goods and services from Canadian plants and Canadian businesses to a larger market that will somehow benefit all Canadians, and it is not happening.
What do they say? They are going to renegotiate and make it better. Let us listen carefully to their list of items to be renegotiated. It dances around the edge. Yes, we agree that the dispute settling mechanism should be improved, that we should be exempted from anti-dumping legislation and all that. However when the Liberals say they are going to renegotiate conjures up a picture that is ridiculous to anybody in Windsor who knows anything about negotiation. I can just imagine the CAW sitting down with Ford and saying: "Hey, folks, we have a contract but we do not want to break it. We just want to renegotiate it".
Ordinarily my colleague from Windsor West is an astute person, but he was almost swallowing his words in uttering such a ridiculous concept as renegotiating without abrogating. What will they do? They are going to renegotiate. They will say: "What are the Americans going to give up?" Are the Americans going to give up complete access to our energy? As a country that has the greatest energy requirements of any industrial nation, the largest nation in the world, the coldest nation of the
world, we have given them access to our energy at our prices. Are the Americans going to give that up? Are the Americans going to give up their access to government procurement? Are the Americans going to give up the elimination of performance rules? Are the Americans going to give up access to unprocessed wood, minerals and fish?
It is difficult to imagine how otherwise intelligent people could propose to the Canadians that they are going to renegotiate a deal without abrogation.
Now they are going to say that New Democrats are trying to build walls. We build walls only high enough to ensure that trade is balanced and fair and to ensure that corporations pay their share of the benefits in infrastructure and everything else on the basis upon which they make profits.
We will abrogate the deal, and if NAFTA is approved this legislation will be abrogated. That is what the Canadian people want. They do not want wishy-washy Liberals who from one day to the next cannot figure out what side they are on because their leader cannot decide which part of the caucus he is going to follow. We know where we stand. We stand for Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise today to speak on Bill C-115, an act to implement the North American free trade agreement.
From a personal perspective my riding is still reeling from the after shock of the current free trade deal earthquake with the United States. Companies and the people who work in them are worried and concerned that a North American agreement will only compound the problems and add to the misery of lost jobs, lost hope and lost opportunities.
At the outset I congratulate my colleague from Etobicoke North for leading the way in this debate. His speech of two months ago was crystal clear and had a great deal of the foresight Canadians are demanding from elected politicians.
It is fantastic that we can debate the true merits of a proposal without being dragged down by partisan interests. However it is worth pointing out that we in the Official Opposition are not a protectionist party like the NDP that wants to hide behind oppressive, unwieldy regulations and red tape.
May 26, 1993

We in the Liberal Party realize the facts of the real world. Canada is a trading nation. It was yesterday. It is today and it forever shall be. Therefore we must negotiate trade agreements that are in the best interests of all Canadians.
We in the Liberal Party urge the government to take advantage of the three-way trade talks to protect Canada's interest and correct the major flaws in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. After Germany we are the leading per capita trading nation in the world. It is in our best interest to have a trade deal that can best utilize our competitive advantage in this unstoppable era of globalization.
I believe Canadians can compete in the emerging global economy but weasel words and statements written by public relation experts of the government appealing to our entrepreneurial spirit and great hopes for the future are not consistent with the facts.
The government, despite its grand intentions, cannot throw our workers to the wolves but must back them up with solid economic policies. The NAFTA does not go far enough in correcting the FTA's flaws. Therefore we cannot support it. This is not a done deal.
President Bill Clinton wants action on environmental and labour standards. We certainly appreciate his support of the Liberal Party's position.
Secure access to the American market was the government's key objective in the FTA, one it failed to achieve. There is still no subsidy or anti-dumping code in the NAFTA. This leaves Canadian industries still exposed to ongoing U.S. trade harassment of the type we have already witnessed with our softwood lumber, steel and magnesium.
Once again there is a complete lack of comprehensive adjustment programs for our firms and our workers. Apparently the government did not learn the lessons of the serious economic fall-out of the 1988 trade deal.
It has no game plan to create jobs and help Canadian workers adapt to this new reality. Even with Mexico on side the government has failed to get the U.S. to allow trade sanctions against countries using low environmental standards to attract investment. Under the NAFTA
Government Orders
environmental protection will be left to a country's best endeavours. What a cop out.
Once again the government knuckled under to U.S. pressure, especially in the vital energy section. Under the NAFTA in times of shortage Canada will still be required to supply the American energy market. Mexico by contrast will retain full control of its energy reserves.
While the FTA's dispute settlement panels, formerly only a temporary measure, have been made permanent they are still not binding in all cases. Nothing in the NAFTA will speed up the lengthy and costly dispute process which was the major flaw of the FTA.
There are some good things in the agreement. The Liberals had called for an accession clause that would allow other western hemisphere nations to join the trading area without a major reworking of NAFTA. The agreement allows for this and gives each country a say over future members.
The auto industry is crucial to my riding of Kent in southwestern Ontario. It is responsible for nearly one-quarter of all the jobs in the city of Chatham. As a result I have looked at the auto parts provisions very closely. The measure to have tighter rules of origin for autos is positive.
The auto pact is preserved. There is a requirement of 62.5 per cent North American content, in two stages over eight years, for light vehicles, their engines and transmissions and 60 per cent for other auto goods to qualify for duty free access to the U.S. and Mexican markets.
New plants will have five years to reach the new content level and major plant refits will have two years. After 10 years there will be the elimination of the Mexican auto decree, which has distorted investment and restricted imports. Canada will retain its high safety and emission standards with the removal of Mexican tariffs on most auto parts within five years and on all auto products within 10 years.
We have a serious trade deficit with Mexico and that hopefully will even out over the years. However according to the Institute for International Economics Canada will be the only nation to suffer under a NAFTA. They predict that Mexico will gain 600,000 jobs and the U.S. will gain 130,000 jobs while we stand to lose 5,000 jobs.

May 26, 1993

We are entering uncharted territory, as was outlined by my colleague from Etobicoke North. We cannot support this deal as it now stands. I am appalled that the government would cut off debate so it can clear the slate for its leadership convention without the new and temporary leader being too tainted with ugly old policies.
