Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to take part in this extremely important debate on the North American free trade agreement.
I submit that the debate we are having today is but the continuation of the one we started in 1988. In fact, the arguments put forward are the same. I was one of those who maintained at the time that it was imperative to have control mechanisms to monitor American investments in Canada. The best example I can think of is still the one where Americans would take over our banks and that would be the end of the Canadian identity.
If they control the banks, and thereby the economy, that will be the end of us, a process which has already begun in the sense that some 350,000 jobs have gone to the United States over the past four years as well as thousands and thousands of businesses.
If they control the export of profits, that too will mean the end of us because, once the Americans start investing more steadily in our Canadian businesses, profits will obviously go to the United States. We would need to monitor that. With profits flowing out of the country,
Canadian companies will certainly lack the financial resources to remain at the leading edge of technology and also to upgrade the training of our professionals, not only the workers but management as well.
It is important to point out that Canada ranks eleventh in the world with respect to management and manpower training.
It is also very disappointing to lose to the United States some of our finest brains, our best scientists and intellectuals. Which brings me to the specific matter of the deficiencies in NAFTA. I think that NAFTA seeks to impose an artificial compatibility on our three countries. First of all, the occupational health and safety standards are very different and workers protection would be disregarded for the sake of profits. Eventually, salaries will be levelled down, which means that Canadian salaries are bound to drop while those in the United States will rise until they finally match ours. Will we lower our environmental standards to meet those of the Americans and the Mexicans?
Today we can give a much more precise meaning to the term "harmonization" as President Reagan and our Prime Minister used it when they sat down to negotiate the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement.
Just think of the comparisons made with respect to the Canadian UI system, the wage loss insurance in the United States and our health care system in which two or three Tory leadership candidates advocate introducing user fees like the ones they have in the United States. In the end, this harmonization is far from natural. Ultimately, our culture will be so diluted and our economy so Americanized that it will undermine our identity as Canadians and our reputation as a nation which knows how to take care of its people.
The North American free trade accord will also increase economic dependency. Let me explain. At present, we export about 80 per cent of our manufactured products to the United States.
Why should we leave the door wide open to American investment and to the migration of Canadian workers and businesses, just for the remaining 20 per cent? In the long run-in a not so distant future, considering that our balance of trade is narrowing-exports and imports will
May 26, 1993

be so closely balanced that you will hardly see the difference between the two countries.
Logic would also dictate that we concentrate much more on improving and promoting relations with countries like China, with its billion plus population, instead of limiting our focus to a small country like Mexico. In the long run, it is important to make sure that our country always remains independent and that exterior economic forces are not allowed to dictate our future economic policies to us.

The more I think of it this debate is a huge exercise in futility because this Conservative government will use its majority to force its erroneous will upon Canadians, the majority of whom do not accept this free trade agreement.
It is futile also in the sense that President Clinton, while campaigning last year, made it very clear that unless there are parallel accords on labour standards and the environment there will be no deals.
Why the rush today when the American Congress has not even been seized with this NAFTA bill? Most important of all, why rush into passing the NAFTA deal in this House when four years after signing the free trade agreement a committee has not even been struck to define the word subsidy or what criteria will constitute dumping? Both agreements rest totally on these two definitions. They are crucial to NAFTA's vitality if it ever happens.
There is also the dispute settlement mechanism which is totally based on American law.
I was talking about the subsidy a while ago. Today as soon as Americans suspect a Canadian product is subsidized they cry murder. Every time it goes to the tribunal, this allegation is judged according to American law. While it is at the tribunal some countervail actions are instituted. There is a serious time delay between the action itself and the verdict of the tribunal which causes enormous loss of revenue. The softwood lumber issue comes to mind. Today there are millions and millions of dollars in the United States still outstanding which belong to Canadian companies.

In my view the free trade agreement of 1988 and this NAFTA deal are both one-way streets to the United States. Businesses and jobs are lined up to go to the United States and I fail, as do my colleagues in the Liberal Party, to recognize any value that it would have for Canadians.

In particular, I have paid special attention to some of the things that have been said by my Liberal colleagues and I would like to comment on some of those things because they deserve comment and clarification.
Not so long ago a Liberal member was up on his feet. The one sentence that caught my ear was this: "The Liberals will work to improve NAFTA". He was speaking as if some day they might form the government. It is not the hon. member who is sitting there wondering whether I am talking about him. It was about two Liberal members ago.
He said that the Liberals will work to improve NAFTA. That is nice but what does it mean? What it sounds like to me is that the Liberals have no intention of not implementing NAFTA should they become the government at the time of the next general election.
What we want to hear from the Liberals and what a great many people who are opposed to NAFTA want to hear from the Liberals is not whether they are opposed to NAFTA or whether they will try to improve NAFTA. It is whether they will or will not implement NAFTA should they have the opportunity to form the government before January 1, 1994. That is the key question.
That is something that we have not heard, yet we have heard dozens of Liberal members who rose to speak. To my knowledge not one of them has said that if the Liberal Party forms the Government of Canada in the next general election then the Liberal Party will not implement NAFTA as of January 1, 1994.

Government Orders
Unless the Liberals are prepared to say that then it seems to me that Canadians who oppose NAFTA are duty bound to look elsewhere to a party that is committed to not implementing NAFTA if it forms the government. That of course is the position of the New Democratic Party.
One will not be able to improve NAFTA if one is willing to implement it on January 1, 1994 and then hope somehow that it can be changed. This is the same unrealistic and misleading position that the Liberals want people to accept with respect to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, that somehow it can be improved on the basis of some future renegotiation.
I think the member from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca said it very well pursuant to an amendment that he moved earlier in this debate. He asked the government to support an amendment that would put into the Canadian legislation the same qualifier with respect to the supremacy of Canadian law over the agreement that the Americans have in their legislation about the supremacy of American law with respect to the trade agreement.
It is that kind of thing that the Americans are not going to be willing to give up. In fact the Liberal position on this with respect to NAFTA and the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement is not to renegotiate in any positive sense but simply to tinker with the terms of surrender.
If we get a Liberal government we will have nothing other than a Vichy regime or a collaborationist regime. This would be a phoney independence. The Leader of the Opposition would be the Marshall Petain of Canadian nationalism who will when push comes to shove do the bidding of his friends in the corporate elite and the people in the BCNI and others who always cover their bets by giving the same amount of money to the Liberals as they give to the Conservatives.
I listened with interest earlier to the Leader of the Opposition and to his attack on the NDP. What did he have to say? It reminded me of the constitutional debates in 1981 when the now Leader of the Opposition was the Minister of Justice and was the official hit man for the Liberals on the Constitution.
I remember those debates, and perhaps you will too, Mr. Speaker, because I know you are just riveted by what I have to say here. Perhaps one remembers when the Leader of the Opposition was the Minister of Justice and the official hit man for the Liberals on the Constitution and how everything was reduced to a simple black and white. If one had a position with respect to the charter of rights where one was considering that maybe there should be a notwithstanding clause or it should not have absolute supremacy-there were a number of nuances as to how a charter of rights might be put into the Constitution-then one was against rights for the Canadians. One was against rights, period.
I listened to the Leader of the Opposition today. If one disagrees with the position on the FTA and NAFTA then one is against trade. Now the NDP is against trade and we want to put walls up around Canada. We never said anything like that. When did we say that?
There is a difference between wanting to get rid of these agreements and putting up walls around Canada. It is precisely the opposite. What we would like to do is create a global trading regime in which the workers of one country are not played off against the workers of another country, in which the tax system of one country is not played off against the tax system of another country, in which we would have global rules that benefit the peoples of all the different countries of the world rather than the corporations that have no respect for the welfare of the peoples of the world or for that matter the sovereign elected governments of the nations of the world.
Is that building walls around Canada? Yet that is the caricature that the Leader of the Opposition wanted to suggest with respect to the NDP position.
We have always supported fair trading arrangements. Who has not? The question is whether or not the free trade agreement is a fair trading arrangement. We say no. We say that the only way a fair trading arrangement can be accomplished is to get out of the FTA and the NAFTA and that is where the difference lies between the NDP and the Liberals. We say that one is dreaming in Technicolor if one thinks that one can renegotiate these agreements.
This is not the only trade arrangement. These agreements are not the only option. That is where one is blind. That is where one is myopic when it comes to this. One

thinks that one can only deal with what one has. We like to dream a little bigger.
We like to think that in the international arena and in the multilateral trading arena we could work with others who want fair trade and not just a playground for the multinationals. We could build that kind of system at the GATT or in some other context because even at the GATT we find the United States trying to impose its version of fair trade on the rest of the world. It is not a question of the FTA and NAFTA or the GATT. Both of them have become a venue for the American world view which is trying to get rid of orderly marketing and trying to get rid of a variety of things that the Americans find objectionable but which we in Canada have found intrinsic to our social and economic well-being.
It does not serve anybody well for the Liberals, for the Conservatives or for us for that matter, to simplify the choices. We are taking a very well-defined position. We are saying that we will not be able to renegotiate these agreements to the satisfaction of Canada. The only way that they could possibly be renegotiated would be for the Americans to actually end up with more than they already have. The only way to do that and the only way to get out of this is to get out of it.
That is the position the Liberals do not agree with. Fair enough. They can say that. They can that they do not agree with that, but they do not and should not say that that implies putting walls up around Canada because that is not what we are talking about.
In fact, some could argue that what the FTA and the NAFTA tried to do was to put walls around North America, that this trading bloc way of thinking about the world is in fact a fortress mentality. Except the fortress is in Canada and the fortress is North America. It is going to be a weakened fortress because within it we will have this reality called Mexico drawing down the social and economic standards and values of the other parts of North America.
I do not think that the Liberal Party does this country any service when it tries to suggest that people who do not agree with it are into building walls around Canada. What we want is a truly global trading system, but we want one that builds up a global community. We want

Mr. Speaker, we are the original free traders. Our original proposals on free trade throughout the history of government in this country were fiercely opposed by the Conservatives in the early 1900s.
We could have a major debate about our position on trade but I think that it is fairly academic considering it is common knowledge just exactly where each party sits with regard to the free trade agreement as well as the North American free trade agreement itself.
I want to speak about some specifics, one being our aim at amending the North American free trade agreement. It is our intention to have the side deals completed and to negotiate the best deal possible. This is no great mystery. We are not opposed to free trade and supportive of blind protectionism, closing our eyes to the opportunities available to us with our world trading partners. No, that is not our position. We want a deal that secures the appropriate provisions on environmental and labour standards.

May 26, 1993
Government Orders
We have to look at this deal from my constituents' perspective, securing perhaps at a later date circumpolar trade links with the former Soviet Union, Greenland and other circumpolar nations. In fact, we have already carried out many exchanges with the former Soviet Union under various protocols signed by our governments in Canada.
My main focus in this debate is on the importance of water in relationship to this trade deal with respect to First Nations and northerners. The issue of water within NAFTA is one which could prove to be extremely critical and is an issue which has yet to be challenged. There have been growing concerns about the role water will play within this agreement, but nothing substantive at this time.
There have been concerns expressed by the Rawson Academy of Aquatic Science and other credible sources that "without an exclusion water is certainly part of the agreement. Any good or service covered by a tariff heading annexed to NAFTA is subject to the rights and obligations set out in the agreement itself. The large-scale movement of water was neither raised nor negotiated during the North American free trade agreement negotiations".
In addition, the Rawson analysis indicates that it also appears that indirect controls on water exports-by the Canadian government-are made more difficult through NAFTA's general investment and national treatment provisions. The report goes on to state that the Canadian government has recognized that water is a good.
The statement of the International Conference on Water and the Environment held in Dublin in 1992 was adopted by representatives from 100 countries, including Canada. One of the statement's four basic principles is: "Water has an economic value in all its competing uses, and should be recognized as an economic good".
The Rawson Academy report on NAFTA and water exports has made a number of recommendations that if the passage of NAFTA goes ahead without the exclusion of water, then three steps must be taken to prevent large-scale water exports.
First, there must be an exemption for large-scale water transfers added to NAFTA itself. Failing this, an
agreement exempting water from NAFTA would have to be negotiated among the parties and this agreement would have to be binding on the trade dispute tribunal or panel.
Second, water must be excluded from the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. As this agreement has already come into force, this would be best assured through a memorandum of understanding between the Canadian and U.S. governments which specifically excludes large-scale water transfers from the agreement.
Third, the federal government needs to pass legislation prohibiting large-scale water exports.
Furthermore, Rawson states the social and economic costs of large-scale water transfers would be extremely high. The cost of compensating people for loss of property and relocation of communities displaced by flooding have been given scant consideration. The burden of these costs would fall largely on Canada's native people who inhabit many of the regions that would be affected by the damming and diversion of northern rivers for water export.
We must not think for a moment that the only demand for water would come from our American neighbours. Mexico is also experiencing a shortage of clean inexpensive sources of water. With over half of Mexico's available supply of fresh water already being consumed by agricultural, industrial and urban activities, it may be safe to say that Mexico will be a net importer of water in the near future.
There has been increasing pressure on Canada to divert its northern water systems. The process of diverting the water of our northern rivers to the southern portion of Canada exists. As an example we have Rafferty-Alameda in Saskatchewan, the Oldman River dam in Alberta and the proposed Assiniboine diversion project in Manitoba.
Another example is the idea of constructing the Grand Canal. Originally proposed in 1964 and considered a good business opportunity by some today, the project would involve the construction of a dam across the mouth of James Bay, converting the bay into a freshwater reservoir and channelling the water via a series of lifts and canals to the Great Lakes and beyond.
All of those diversion schemes are highly adaptable to transferring large quantities of water across to the U.S.

There is also the whole area of just exactly what the value of water is to many of our aboriginal communities. In the area where I live we have huge bodies of water that have had a historical relationship, one that is very close to the aboriginal population. We have two of the largest lakes in Canada, the Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake. We have 1,800 kilometres of the Mackenzie River which flows right into the Arctic Ocean. We have many other sources of water in the Northwest Territories.
I could talk about water for quite a period of time, but I just want to make the point that this whole issue has gone unchallenged and needs to be mentioned.
With regard to the amendments and side deals that are being made, this trade deal could not only influence the use of our water but our forests as well. This is another area that is extremely important. Free trade may allow for the concentration of processing by megamills that would have no real interest in forest ecosystems.
Industrialization of the forest will result in the development of fast growing, genetically homogenized smaller trees, cropped in fast rotation, replacing our diverse forests with their potential for diverse economics. Forests and the quality of water are integrally related. Healthy forests produce clean water, adequate water supplies and allow forests to prosper. Therefore any industrial depletion of our forests is guaranteed to affect the local and continental water regime.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, many of us have been in this House for a number of hours, some of us around the clock. I think you might find there is disposition now to apply the remaining votes to the one just taken.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Madam Speaker, on the same point of order. I think we would have agreement with what my hon. friend has suggested with one qualification and that is that the vote on the concurrence motion be applied in reverse.

Madam Speaker, I was absent for the last vote. I understand the House needs unanimous consent. I am prepared, Madam Speaker, as long as my vote is applied as my party's vote is applied over the remainder of the votes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand now that there is unanimous consent?
Madam Speaker, on a point of order, as I was absent for the last vote, if the Chamber agrees that all the votes are going to be applied as previously, then I accept.

Madam Speaker, with respect, I would like to point out that we would be willing to apply certain votes to the one just taken. We would vote either yea or nay, depending on the motion. If you want me to give you the list of yeas and nays, in that case we would be agreeable to this procedure.
[DOT]	(2055)

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe I may be able to make things easier for everyone, with the co-operation of the House. I believe there is consent for not proceeding with a recorded division on each motion presented before the House and, subsequently, on the motion for adopting the report stage. I suggest, considering the request made by the hon. member for Saint-Hubert, which is similar to the one made by the hon. member for Calgary-Northeast, that when the Chair has put the question for the last time, the parties come to the Table and indicate exactly on which motions they intended to vote yea or nay. Is it agreed?
Agreed.

Madam Speaker, I would like some clarification. Normally when we do this as a time saving measure we have traditionally stood in our places and told the table our yeas and nays. You are now suggesting that we come to the table later. Is that consistent?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, because of the day that we have all had. I do not mean to make it a precedent. It has been offered by our Clerk that for tonight we come to the table after and do that, just for tonight. I think that everyone agrees that it is a very good idea for tonight. Is it agreed?
Agreed.
